metric_rationale: The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against Tallying. In almost all trials, the option favored by the single most valid discriminating cue (TTB's choice) is opposed by the option that wins on a larger number of less valid cues (Tallying's choice). This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the TTB prediction. TTB will produce values close to 1.0, while Tallying will produce values close to 0.0, creating a massive and highly reliable gap between the two theories.

The chosen experimental design systematically pits Tallying against Take The Best. For 5 out of the 6 unique trials, the two heuristics make diametrically opposed predictions. This metric isolates those discriminating trials by filtering out any trials where Tallying predicts a tie, and computes the proportion of subject responses that align with the Tallying prediction. Data simulated under Tallying will yield values significantly above 0.5 (approaching 1.0 for low noise), whereas data simulated under TTB will yield values significantly below 0.5 (approaching 0.0), ensuring a massive contrast between the two theories with low between-subject variance.

This metric isolates trials where Tallying sees a strict tie (an equal number of feature wins for option A and option B). On these trials, Tallying is completely undiscriminating and predicts uniform guessing (50% accuracy). In contrast, WADD uses the validities (centered at chance) to break these ties, leading to a strong directional preference. By computing the proportion of times the subject's choice aligns with WADD's preference on these Tallying-tie trials, we expect a value near 0.5 for data generated by Tallying, and a value substantially above 0.5 for data generated by WADD.

By isolating specific trials where Tallying and the Weighted Additive Model (WADD) make opposite predictions, we can strongly separate the two theories. In Trial 3 and Trial 6, Tallying favors Option B because it wins on more features, whereas WADD strongly prefers Option A due to the high weight of the first feature. In Trial 5, Tallying prefers Option A for having more winning features, but WADD favors Option B. This metric calculates the average alignment with Tallying's predictions across these three highly discriminative trials. Tallying will yield values significantly above 0.5 (approaching 1.0), whereas WADD will yield values significantly below 0.5 (approaching 0.0).

This metric isolates trials 1, 3, and 4 from the experimental design. In these specific trials, the two options tie in the number of feature wins (Pure Tallying predicts a 50/50 guess), but one option strictly dominates the other in terms of feature validities regardless of the non-linear scaling parameter gamma. The Advocated Theory's tie-breaking mechanism therefore deterministically favors the validity-dominant option. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the tie-breaker's prediction on these unambiguous trials, we expect the Advocated Theory to yield a value significantly above 0.5, while Pure Tallying will center tightly around 0.5.

This metric isolates trials where the two options are perfectly tied in the number of winning features (a tallying tie). According to the Advocated Theory (Pure Tallying), subjects have no basis for preference on these trials and must guess, resulting in a 50% alignment with any tie-breaking rule. The Competing Theory, however, postulates a validity-weighted tie-breaker when tallies are tied. The metric calculates the proportion of choices on tied trials that align with the higher validity-weighted option. The Competing Theory will predict a high alignment score (> 0.5), whereas Pure Tallying predicts exactly 0.5.

Pure Tallying relies exclusively on counting feature wins. On trials where the tally difference is exactly zero, Pure Tallying has no basis for preference and predicts a 50/50 guess, resulting in an expected absolute deviation from 0.5 near 0 (modulo binomial sampling noise). The Advocated theory, however, ALWAYS triggers its salience-weighted tie-breaker on these exact ties. Depending on the subject's 'gamma' parameter, the tie-breaker will consistently and strongly favor either the option with more valid features (if gamma > 0) or the option with less valid features (if gamma < 0). By computing the absolute deviation of the choice proportion from 0.5 on these 'exact tie' trials FOR EACH SUBJECT independently, we capture this systematic preference. Pure Tallying will yield a small value (binomial noise), whereas the Advocated theory will yield a large value (close to 0.5).

Pure Tallying treats exact ties in tally as a complete guess, predicting a 50/50 choice probability regardless of the features' validities. This means a subject's empirical choice proportion on exact tie trials will be close to 0.5, with small binomial variance. In contrast, the Competing Theory assumes that a tally difference of 0 always triggers a compensatory tie-breaker. Because the tie-breaker weights features by salience, it will strongly favor one option over the other (which one depends on the subject's gamma parameter). Consequently, the Competing Theory predicts deterministic or near-deterministic choices on these trials, leading to an empirical choice proportion far from 0.5. By computing the absolute deviation of each subject's choice proportion from 0.5 on exact tie trials, we expect a value near 0.1 for Pure Tallying and > 0.3 for the Competing Theory, highly discriminating the two.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option that possesses the most valid feature (feature 1), conditional on only one option having it. The experimental design intentionally pits feature 1 against a larger number of less valid features. Pure Tallying ignores feature validities and strictly counts feature-wise wins, so it systematically chooses the option WITHOUT feature 1 in these trials (scoring near 0). The Advocated Theory (Additive Utility with power-law validities) heavily weights feature 1, causing subjects to systematically choose the option WITH feature 1 (scoring near 1). This provides a massive, stable contrast between the two models.

In Trials 1, 2, and 4, the Pure Tallying heuristic predicts either a preference for Option A (Trial 1) or a 50/50 guess (Trials 2 and 4), because Option A has either more feature-wise wins or an equal number of wins. By contrast, the Additive Utility (WADD) model strongly prefers Option B across all these trials because Option B dominates on the features with the highest objective validities. By calculating the proportion of times Option A is chosen across these specific trials, we expect Tallying to yield a value reliably >= 0.5, whereas WADD will yield a value significantly < 0.5.

In Trial 1, the options are [0, 1, 1, 1, 1] and [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]. The Competing Theory strongly prefers [0, 1, 1, 1, 1] because both Tallying (4 vs 1) and WADD with Bayesian log-odds weights (sum of weights 3.65 vs 2.94) favor it. Thus, it predicts choosing [1, 0, 0, 0, 0] only due to random noise. In contrast, the Advocated Theory uses a power-law transformation of chance-centered validities. For gamma > 2.5, the single most valid cue outweighs the sum of the other four, leading to a strong preference for [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]. Since gamma ranges up to 10, the Advocated Theory predicts a much higher choice proportion for [1, 0, 0, 0, 0] than the Competing Theory.

In Trial 8 (A=[0,0,1,1,1]), the Advocated Theory's Tallying component favors Option A while its WADD component favors Option B, leading to a mixed probability of choosing A. The Competing Theory, however, overwhelmingly favors Option B for any value of its power-law parameter gamma, predicting a near-zero probability for A. Conversely, in Trial 1 (A=[1,0,0,0,0]), the Advocated Theory strongly predicts Option B across both components, whereas the Competing Theory's power-law weighting will often favor Option A when gamma is high. Subtracting the probability of choosing A in Trial 1 from Trial 8 captures this structural divergence, yielding a positive value for the Advocated Theory and a negative or near-zero value for the Competing Theory.

The metric computes the overall proportion of times subjects choose the option with features 2 and 3 (the '01100' option) in Trials 1 and 3. Under the Advocated Theory, validities 0.93 and 0.91 are almost as strong as 0.95, so their combined weight easily outweighs feature 1 (0.95) in Trial 1, and also outweighs features 1, 4, 5 (0.95, 0.60, 0.55) in Trial 3. Thus, the Advocated Theory consistently prefers the '01100' option in both trials, leading to a metric value near 2.0. In contrast, the Competing Theory enforces a strict ordinal drop-off, heavily penalizing ranks 2 and 3. As a result, feature 1 dominates features 2 and 3 in Trial 1, and features 1, 4, 5 dominate features 2 and 3 in Trial 3. The Competing Theory therefore avoids the '01100' option in both trials, yielding a metric value near 0.0.

The experimental design pits the single best feature (Rank 1, validity 0.95) against a combination of slightly less valid features (Ranks 2 and 3, validities 0.90 and 0.85). The Advocated Theory (Rank-Based Weighting) enforces a steep drop-off between Rank 1 and Ranks 2/3, predicting that the option with Feature 1 will be chosen more frequently. In contrast, the Competing Theory (Magnitude-Based Additive Utility) scales weights by chance-centered validities (0.45 vs 0.40 and 0.35), meaning Ranks 2 and 3 combined (0.75) will easily overpower Rank 1 (0.45), leading to fewer choices for the option with Feature 1. This metric simply calculates the overall proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option containing Feature 1, which will robustly discriminate between the two theories.

This metric calculates 2 * P(A|T3) + P(A|T4). Under the Competing Theory (Sequential Evidence Accumulation), this linear combination is a theoretical invariant. For low thresholds (<=1), SEA stops at the first feature, yielding P(A|T3)=1 and P(A|T4)=0, so the sum is 2. For high thresholds (>1), SEA evaluates to the end for T3 (yielding a tie, P=0.5) and strictly prefers A for T4 (P=1), again yielding 2 * 0.5 + 1 = 2. Thus, SEA predicts a constant value of ~1.9 (after epsilon adjustments) with near-zero parameter variance. In contrast, the Advocated Theory (Additive Utility) applies compensatory weighting. For most of its parameter space (gamma > 1), the weights of less valid features decay rapidly, pushing both choice probabilities towards 0.5, which bounds this metric around 1.5. For gamma=1, T3 yields a negative score and T4 a positive score, dropping the metric even lower (towards 1.0). Therefore, the Advocated Theory predicts a significantly lower and tightly bounded value (~1.5) than SEA (~1.9), providing a massive mean gap with exceptionally low between-subject variance for reliable discrimination.

Calculates the sum of the probability of choosing Option A in Trial 2 and Trial 3. Under the Advocated Theory (Sequential Evidence Accumulation), a threshold <= 1 leads to choosing B in T2 and A in T3, while a threshold > 1 leads to choosing A in T2 and B in T3. Thus, for any threshold, the expected sum of P(A|T2) + P(A|T3) is exactly 1.0, resulting in extremely low between-subject variance. Under the Competing Theory (Additive Utility), moderate values of gamma (e.g., gamma around 1 to 3) lead to choosing A in both T2 and T3 due to the power-law weighting of cues, pushing the sum significantly higher than 1.0. This creates a large mean difference and exploits the structural invariance in the Advocated Theory to guarantee a highly significant Welch's t-test.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option favored exclusively by the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy in a specific pair of trials. Specifically, for the pair [1, 0, 0, 1, 1] vs. [0, 1, 1, 0, 0], both Take-The-Best and Tallying favor the first option. Furthermore, the Competing Theory's Sequential Accumulation mechanism also strictly prefers the first option, regardless of its threshold parameter (the accumulated evidence for the first option never drops below 0 and ends at +1). However, the WADD submodel in the Advocated Theory strongly favors the second option [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] because the combined log-odds of features 2 and 3 outweigh features 1, 4, and 5. Therefore, the Advocated Theory predicts a significantly higher choice rate for [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] than the Competing Theory, which will only choose it via random lapses.

By design, Option B wins the most valid cue in all trials, meaning Take-The-Best (and thus the Advocated Theory with a low threshold <= 1) always chooses B. However, for higher thresholds, the Advocated Theory's sequential accumulation can favor Option A. Specifically, a medium threshold (1 < thresh <= 2) triggers early stopping in Trial 1, leading to an Option A choice. A high threshold (thresh > 2) prevents early stopping in Trial 3, allowing the final tally to favor Option A, while still triggering early stopping for Option B in Trial 7. Thus, the Advocated Theory predicts that subjects with threshold > 1 will choose Option A in EITHER Trial 1 OR Trial 3, but not Trial 7. In contrast, the Competing Theory's sub-models either uniformly favor B (Trial 1) or have identical strategy mixtures for Trial 3 and Trial 7 (Tallying favors A, TTB/WADD favor B). Therefore, the metric `P(A|Trial 1) + P(A|Trial 3) - P(A|Trial 7)` will be near 0 for the Competing Theory (since P(A|T3) ≈ P(A|T7) and P(A|T1) ≈ 0), but will be strongly positive (~0.67) for the Advocated Theory, reliably discriminating the two models despite individual parameter differences.

This metric calculates the proportion of times subjects choose the option [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] when it is presented (Trials 1 and 2). For the Competing Theory, the unweighted tally starts at -1 and ends at -1, meaning it structurally must always choose the opposing option [1, 0, 0, 1, 1] regardless of the stopping threshold (barring epsilon noise). For the Advocated Theory, the non-linear weighting of chance-centered validities allows the combination of the 2nd and 3rd features to overpower the 1st, 4th, and 5th features. With a moderate to high threshold, the Advocated Theory will robustly choose the target option [0, 1, 1, 0, 0], creating a stark and highly discriminative contrast.

The metric computes a double difference in the choice proportions of option B across the four trial types. For the Advocated Theory (Unweighted), Trials 1 and 2 structurally force choices of B and A respectively regardless of threshold, making (m1 - m2) strongly positive (~1). Meanwhile, its choices on Trials 3 and 4 depend heavily on the threshold, averaging out across subjects. For the Competing Theory (Weighted), the opposite is true: its choices on Trials 3 and 4 are structurally forced to B and A respectively because the heavy validities align, making (m3 - m4) strongly positive (~1), while Trials 1 and 2 are threshold-dependent. The double difference thus yields opposite signs for the two theories, ensuring strong discrimination.
